discussion_comments.comment_body:
**#6 Low (CONFIRMED): the guard is keyed to the magic number instead of the contract.**

Two gaps:
1. The regex only matches the literal `1000` (the `[[:space:]]*$` tail even excludes `10000`). Pinning `runAsUser: 1001` or any other UID regresses OpenShift arbitrary-UID support while CI stays green. The actual contract this PR establishes is "no `runAsUser` at all in the default render", so grep for the bare key:

```sh
if grep -Eq '^[[:space:]]+runAsUser:' /tmp/helm-template-output.yaml; then
```

2. The default render exercises only the sqlite StatefulSet path (`stateful.yaml`); a `runAsUser` hardcoded into `deployment.yaml` (postgres mode) or `postgresql-deployment.yaml` would go undetected. Consider repeating the assertion on a `--set storage.mode=postgres` render.

discussion_comments.comment_body:
**#3 Medium (CONFIRMED): this advice fails on the platform it names.**

`fsGroup: 0` is outside the namespace-allocated range that restricted-v2's `MustRunAs` fsGroup strategy validates against, and there is no root-group exception in the [fsGroup admission code](https://github.com/openshift/apiserver-library-go/blob/master/pkg/securitycontextconstraints/group/mustrunas.go) (the "GID 0 supplemental group" convention applies to the container's group membership, not the `fsGroup` field). An OpenShift user following this message gets:

```
fsGroup: Invalid value: []int64{0}: 0 is not an allowed group
```

replacing a crash-loop with an admission rejection. Suggested wording:

```sh
echo "  On OpenShift, leave podSecurityContext.fsGroup unset (set it to null in Helm values);"
echo "  the SCC assigns an in-range group. On vanilla Kubernetes with a PVC, set fsGroup"
echo "  (e.g. 1000), or mount a volume writable by GID 0 to match the image's group-0 ownership."
```

discussion_comments.comment_body:
**#5 Low (CONFIRMED): non-root ownership repair silently removed.**

The old script attempted `chown -R` on any uid/gid mismatch without a root check. POSIX allows a non-root owner to chgrp files it owns to any group in its credentials, so compose setups like `user: "1000:2000"` over a volume owned `1000:1000` previously got the tree re-grouped to 2000 at startup; sidecars sharing GID 2000 relied on that. Now the repair is skipped (the writability probe still passes via owner-write, so there is not even a warning) and group-mediated access quietly degrades.

Probably an acceptable trade for dropping CAP_CHOWN, but worth a release-note mention, and consider emitting an informational line when a uid/gid mismatch is detected but left unrepaired as non-root.
